Unit 6: Period 6 (1865–1898)

📋 Everything from Unit 6 in one place — the Gilded Age, 14 topics. Use the animation to lock in labor conflict escalation before your test.
6.1

Contextualizing Period 6

  • Rapid industrialization: the Second Industrial Revolution.
  • Transcontinental Railroad (1869) transforms the economy.
  • Era nicknamed the Gilded Age — glittering surface, serious problems beneath.
Second Industrial RevolutionGilded Age
Period 6 at a glance.
6.2

Westward Expansion: Economic Development

  • Homestead Act (1862) grants land to settlers.
  • Railroads, mining booms, and the cattle industry drive Western growth.
Homestead Act
Drivers of Western development.
6.3

Westward Expansion: Social & Cultural

  • Diverse settlers: European immigrants, Chinese laborers, Black “exodusters.”
  • Dawes Act (1887): breaks up tribal land into individual allotments — forced assimilation.
  • “Frontier myth” romanticized expansion, obscuring the violence involved.
ExodustersDawes Act
Social & cultural change in the West.
6.4

The “New South”

  • Promise: diversified, industrialized economy. Reality: stayed cotton-dependent.
  • Sharecropping trapped many farmers in debt.
  • Jim Crow laws + poll taxes/literacy tests enforced segregation & disenfranchisement.
SharecroppingJim Crow laws
Promise vs. reality.
6.5

Technological Innovation

  • Bessemer process: cheap, abundant steel → skyscrapers, railroads.
  • Telephone (1876), electric light (1879) transform industry & daily life.
Bessemer process
Innovation fuels industry.
6.6

The Rise of Industrial Capitalism

  • Vertical integration (Carnegie): controls every production stage.
  • Horizontal integration (Rockefeller): buys out competitors.
  • Social Darwinism: “survival of the fittest” justifies wealth gaps.
Vertical integrationSocial Darwinism
Trap: Vertical = controls all stages (Carnegie/steel); Horizontal = absorbs competitors at one stage (Rockefeller/oil).
Strategies of industrial capitalism.
6.7

Labor in the Gilded Age

  • Dangerous conditions → workers organize (Knights of Labor, AFL).
  • Major strikes: Great Railroad Strike (1877), Homestead (1892), Pullman (1894).
  • Government/business often sided against strikers.
Knights of LaborPullman Strike
Labor organizing & conflict.

6.8

Immigration/Migration in the Gilded Age

  • “Old” immigration: Northern/Western Europe. “New” immigration (post-1880): Southern/Eastern Europe, Asia.
  • Driven by push factors (poverty, persecution) & pull factors (jobs, freedom).
Push/pull factors
Old vs. new immigration.
6.9

Responses to Immigration

  • Nativism & the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) — hostility toward immigrants.
  • Settlement houses (Jane Addams's Hull House) & Americanization programs support/assimilate immigrants.
Chinese Exclusion ActHull House
Hostility & support.
6.10

Development of the Middle Class

  • New white-collar jobs (managers, clerks) grow with industrialization.
  • New consumer culture: department stores, mail-order catalogs.
White-collar jobs
A consumer middle class.
6.11

Reform in the Gilded Age

  • Social Gospel: reform as a Christian duty. Settlement houses, temperance.
  • Pendleton Act (1883): merit-based hiring, in response to Garfield's assassination.
Social GospelPendleton Act
Gilded Age reform movements.
6.12

Controversies over the Role of Government

  • Laissez-faire: government should not interfere in the economy.
  • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): aimed to break up monopolies, but weakly enforced.
Laissez-faireSherman Antitrust Act
Debating government's economic role.
6.13

Politics in the Gilded Age

  • Patronage system: jobs awarded by political loyalty, not merit.
  • Populist Party (1892): farmers demand free silver, railroad regulation.
Patronage systemPopulist Party
Gilded Age political developments.
6.14

Continuity and Change in Period 6

  • Change: U.S. becomes a leading industrial power; massive immigration reshapes cities.
  • Continuity: racial inequality persists (Jim Crow); conflict with Native nations continues.
Continuity and change
1865–1898.

Master Summary Table

TermKey Distinction

⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • The Sherman Antitrust Act was used more often against labor unions than actual monopolies in its early years.
  • Social Darwinism justified inequality; the Social Gospel argued the opposite — that Christians should fix inequality.
  • The Dawes Act broke up tribal land into individual plots — don't confuse with the earlier Indian Removal Act.
  • Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first major law to restrict immigration by nationality/race specifically.
  • The Pendleton Act followed directly from Garfield's assassination by a disappointed office-seeker.
  • Economic change in this period outpaced social/political change — labor protections and racial equality lagged behind industrial growth.
